marble.name: Conduction, convection, and radiation
marble.subject: Science
marble.description: Describe and compare the three mechanisms of heat transfer — conduction (particle vibration through solids), convection (fluid movement in liquids/gases), and radiation (infrared waves) — and explain that the rate of transfer depends on temperature difference
marble.prompt: If you was heating soup on a hob and also warming their hands by a radiator, could they explain which type of heat transfer is happening in each case — and why the soup pot gets hot throughout even though it’s only heated at the bottom?

cluster.summary: Your child is beginning to understand energy — observing how sunlight warms objects and surfaces, and designing simple structures to create shade and reduce warming effects.

misconceptions: 'Cold flows / cold gets in' — treating cold as a substance that travels. Energy only ever moves from hotter to cooler; a cold object gains energy, it does not emit cold.
'Heat rises' — over-generalised. It is warmed FLUID (less dense air/water) that rises in convection; heat itself has no inherent upward direction, and conduction/radiation are not 'up'.
Confusing temperature with heat / thermal energy — temperature measures average particle kinetic energy; a large warm object can hold more thermal energy than a small hot one.
'Metal is colder than wood' — objects in the same room are at the same temperature; metal merely conducts energy away from the hand faster, so it FEELS colder.
'Convection is heat moving through the liquid/gas' — in convection the fluid itself physically circulates; the energy is carried by moving matter, not passed through stationary matter.
representations: Particle diagram of conduction — a row of fixed, vibrating particles passing energy along to neighbours; free electrons added for metals to show why metals cond
Convection-current loop — a cross-section (beaker or room) with arrows showing warmed fluid expanding, becoming less dense, rising, cooling and sinking; the MAT
Infrared radiation arrows across a gap / vacuum — wavy IR emitted and absorbed with no medium; thermal-imaging (false-colour) photos.
The metal-vs-wood 'same temperature, different feel' demo — separating temperature from rate of conduction and from sensation.
Leslie cube / surface-colour comparison — matt black vs shiny silver faces emitting/absorbing IR at different rates.
A temperature-difference → rate dial: bigger difference = faster transfer; the cooling curve that steepens with a larger gap and flattens as equilibrium nears.
authoredAnswer: No — both are at the same room temperature. The metal feels colder because it's a good conductor: it conducts heat away from your warm hand quickly, so your hand cools fast and feels the loss. Wood is a poor conductor, so it draws heat from your hand slowly and feels warmer. Feeling is about the RATE heat leaves your hand, not the object's temperature.
probe: Put out a metal spoon and a wooden spoon that have shared the same room. Ask the child to predict what a thermometer (or thermal strip) will read on each — different or the same — AND why. The 'metal is colder' child predicts a lower reading on the metal; the conduction child predicts equal readings. Then measure both

wrongAnswers.wrong: The metal spoon really is colder than the wooden one, because metal is a cold material.
wrongAnswers.revealedBy: Says the two objects are at different temperatures, or that metal contains cold.
wrongAnswers.fix: Measure both with a thermometer — same temperature; reframe the feeling as heat leaving the hand fast through a good conductor.

wrongAnswers.wrong: The cold flows out of the metal and into your hand, which is why it feels cold.
wrongAnswers.revealedBy: Describes cold travelling into the hand rather than heat leaving it.
wrongAnswers.fix: Only energy (heat) moves, always hot→cold; 'cold' isn't a thing that flows — your hand loses heat to the metal.

wrongAnswers.revealedBy: Explains a convection current as 'heat goes up', with no mention of density or fluid movement.
wrongAnswers.fix: The heated fluid expands, becomes less dense and rises; cooler denser fluid sinks — it's the fluid that moves, carrying energy.
